title: A validator must assume that the Spell Team answering their question is lying to conceal an attack
content:
A.1.10.2.4.12.4.4 states the posture without hedging: when an issue is raised, "the Core Facilitator or the Spell Team who worked on the Spell is likely to respond to the issue. **The Spell validator must assume that the parties providing the answer are acting maliciously and lying to prevent the discovery of their attack.**"

This is a deliberate inversion of professional norms. Normally a subject-matter expert's explanation resolves a reviewer's question, and continuing to doubt them after a credible answer is rude. The Atlas makes that doubt mandatory.

The reason is that a real attacker is precisely the party best equipped to produce a reassuring explanation. They know the code, they anticipated the question, and their answer will be more fluent and more confident than a genuine mistake's would be. Under a good-faith default, the most dangerous case is the one most easily talked past.

The operative consequence is in the next sentence: "The validator may only consider the issue as resolved once they are comfortable that the issue does not constitute a bug or attack." Resolution requires the validator's own understanding, not the answerer's assurance — an explanation is a hypothesis to verify, not evidence.

It is also a social protection. Refusing to accept a senior engineer's word is costly for an individual to do on their own initiative; making it the written rule means a validator who keeps pushing is complying with process rather than being difficult. The same technique appears at A.1.10.2.4.9.2.1, which pre-labels anyone urging a shortcut as negligent or malicious.
description: A.1.10.2.4.12.4.4 replaces good-faith presumption with adversarial default, so a plausible explanation from the authors is not by itself grounds to close an issue.
